newsitem.title: USA: High Court to hear SEC insider-trading appeal.
newsitem.headline: High Court to hear SEC insider-trading appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court said Friday it would hear a Justice Department appeal of a ruling rejecting one of the federal government's key weapons in cracking down on insider-trading abuses.

The high court acted on a Justice Department appeal, filed on behalf of the Securities and Exchange Commission, of a ruling that overturned a lawyer's insider-trading conviction related to a 1988 Grand Metropolitan Plc takeover bid.

The U.S. appeals court ruling in August dealt a setback to the "misappropriation theory" of securities law, which the government has employed against those who use sensitive, secret information, but are not traditional company insiders.
Under the theory, if a person misappropriates inside information and trades on it, that is illegal under the securities law because the person has breached a trust.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the closely watched securities case in April, with a decision due by the end of its term in late June.
"We're very pleased with the Supreme Court's decision to hear this important case and expect a decision by the court before the end of the term," SEC lawyer Paul Gonson said.
The appeals court overturned the conviction of James O'Hagan, a Minneapolis lawyer whose firm had been retained by Grand Metropolitan in connection with its 1988 takeover of Pillsbury Co.
He was convicted of using secret information about the deal to reap a $4.3 million profit in Pillsbury stock and stock options. He was sentenced to 41 months in prison.

The St. Louis-based appeals court reversed his conviction on the grounds that he had not violated any fiduciary duty to Pillsbury stockholders. The court said his conduct was unethical and immoral, but not illegal.
The law at issue has been used in a number of high-profile cases against people who were not considered company insiders.

Those cases include a printer of secret tender offer documents, a psychiatrist who learned from a patient of a takeover bid and former Wall Street Journal reporter R. Foster Winans, who leaked confidential information before it appeared in a widely read stocks column.

In appealing to the Supreme Court, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said the appellate court's ruling will "critically weaken the government's ability to prosecute the misuse of material, nonpublic information in the securities markets."

He warned that the ruling has "opened a large loophole in the protections against fraud afforded by federal law," and said it will hurt investor confidence in the integrity of the nation's securities markets.
Dellinger said the decision conflicts with rulings by other appeals courts around the country and by the Supreme Court.
An attorney for O'Hagan urged the Supreme Court to deny the appeal, saying the misappropriation theory should not be applied to criminal cases because of its uncertain legal status.
